result.formulation:
CITATION CHECK: the believed reference is correct. Title "Warm-starting quantum optimization"; authors Daniel J. Egger, Jakub Mareček (háček on the c; arXiv listing prints "Marecek"), Stefan Woerner; Quantum 5, 479 (2021), published 2021-06-17; DOI 10.22331/q-2021-06-17-479; arXiv:2009.10095. Confirmed on the arXiv abstract page, the Quantum journal page, and Crossref.

All equations below are from arXiv v4 (the Quantum version), full PDF text.

--- Sec. 2.1 Preliminaries ---
(QUBO): min_{x in {0,1}^n} x^T Σ x + μ^T x, "where x is a vector of n binary decision variables, Σ ∈ R^{n×n} a symmetric matrix, and μ ∈ R^n a vector."
(QP): "If Σ is positive semidefinite, the trivial continuous relaxation of QUBO   min_{x in [0,1]^n} x^T Σ x   (QP)   is a convex quadratic program and the optimal solution c* of the continuous relaxation is easily obtainable with classical optimizers [64]."
(SDP), used when Σ is not PSD: max_{Y in S^n} tr(ΣY), subject to diag(Y) = e, Y ⪰ 0. (The paper writes "max" here although (QUBO) is a "min"; quoted as printed.)

--- Sec. 2.2 Continuous warm-start QAOA ---
Variable/qubit relation: x_i = (1 − z_i)/2, each z_i replaced by Z_i.
Eq. (1): |φ*> = ⊗_{i=0}^{n−1} R_Y(θ_i) |0>_n, with θ_i = 2 arcsin( sqrt(c_i*) ), c_i* in [0,1] the i-th coordinate of the optimum of (QP). "The probability to measure |1> in qubit i is thus c_i*".
Eq. (2): the standard mixer H_M = −Σ_i X_i is replaced by H_M^(ws) = Σ_i H_{M,i}^(ws) with
  H_{M,i}^(ws) = [[ 2c_i* − 1 ,  −2 sqrt(c_i*(1−c_i*)) ],
                  [ −2 sqrt(c_i*(1−c_i*)) ,  1 − 2c_i* ]]
"and has R_Y(θ_i)|0> as ground state with eigenvalue of −1. The ground state of H_M^(ws) is thus |φ*> with eigenvalue −n".
Mixing gate: exp(−i β_k H_M^(ws)). "Since H_{M,i}^(ws) = −sin(θ_i) X − cos(θ_i) Z the time-evolved mixing Hamiltonian is a rotation around the axis n = [−sin(θ_i), 0, −cos(θ_i)] on the Bloch-sphere of qubit i and can be implemented using the single-qubit rotations R_Y(θ_i) R_Z(−2β) R_Y(−θ_i)."
This is an OPERATOR product (rightmost acts first). Fig. 2 draws the circuit in time order as R_Y(θ_i) [state prep] -> e^{−iγ_k H_C} -> R_Y(−θ_i) -> R_Z(−2β_k) -> R_Y(θ_i), repeated p times.
Regularisation (unnumbered, Sec. 2.2), ε in [0, 0.5]:
  θ_i = 2 arcsin(sqrt(c_i*))   if c_i* in [ε, 1−ε],
  θ_i = 2 arcsin(sqrt(ε))      if c_i* ≤ ε,
  θ_i = 2 arcsin(sqrt(1−ε))    if c_i* ≥ 1−ε.
"The mixer Hamiltonian is adjusted accordingly." At ε = 0.5 the initial state is the equal superposition and the mixer is the X operator.

--- Sec. 2.3 Rounded warm-start QAOA ---
Initial state: from a given GW cut, "using Y-rotations with a ε ∈ (0, 0.5), as discussed in Sec. 2.2" (i.e. the binary c_i in {0,1} is clipped to ε or 1−ε, same formula for θ_i).
Mixer is DIFFERENT from the continuous case: time evolution R_Y(−θ_i) R_Z(−2β) R_Y(θ_i) "instead of" R_Y(θ_i) R_Z(−2β) R_Y(−θ_i), "i.e., we multiply the off-diagonal elements in (2) by −1."
Eq. (3): with ε = 0.25, β_1 = π/2, γ_1 = 0 the depth-one variational form reduces, per qubit, to
  R_Y(−θ_i) R_Z(−π) R_Y(2θ_i) |0>,
which "creates the states −i|1> and −i|0> when c_i* = ε and 1 − ε, respectively."
(For ε = 0.25: θ_i = π/3 when c = ε and 2π/3 when c = 1−ε.)

--- Sec. 3 portfolio problem (continuous warm start test) ---
Eq. (4)-(5): min_{x in {0,1}^n} q x^T Σ x − μ^T x such that 1^T x = B; budget enforced by penalty λ(1^T x − B)^2.

--- Sec. 4 MAXCUT (rounded warm start test) ---
Eq. (6): max (1/2) Σ_{(i,j) in E} ω_ij (1 − z_i z_j), z in {−1,1}^{|V|}.
Appendix B (GW): relaxation Eq. (7) max (1/2) Σ_{i<j} ω_ij (1 − v_i^T v_j) with unit vectors v_i; rounding z_i = sign(r^T v_i*) with r uniform on the unit sphere.
Appendix F (depth-one simulation) gives the cost gate for the ω_ij Z_i Z_j term as U_{i,j} = diag(1, e^{iγω_ij}, e^{iγω_ij}, 1), and the mixer as e^{−iβ H_M^(ws)}.

--- Numerical checks I ran (numpy/scipy, Qiskit gate definitions RY(t)=exp(−itY/2), RZ(t)=exp(−itZ/2)), all to ~1e-14 ---
(a) Eq. (2) matrix == −sinθ X − cosθ Z for θ = 2 arcsin(sqrt c).
(b) RY(θ) RZ(−2β) RY(−θ) == exp(−iβ H_{M,i}^(ws)) exactly (no global phase).
(c) RY(θ)|0> = sqrt(1−c)|0> + sqrt(c)|1>, eigenvalue −1 of H_{M,i}^(ws).
(d) RY(−θ) RZ(−2β) RY(θ) == exp(−iβ(+sinθ X − cosθ Z)) (the rounded/modified mixer).
(e) Eq. (3) gives exactly −i|1> for c = 0.25 and −i|0> for c = 0.75.
result.sign_conventions:
The paper MINIMISES and uses exactly our signs.

- Objective: (QUBO) is a "min". The introduction says the algorithm encodes the problem "in a Hamiltonian H_C whose ground state is the optimum solution" and a classical optimizer seeks β, γ "to create a trial state which minimizes the energy of the Hamiltonian H_C".
- Layer: "a quantum circuit applies exp(−iβ_k H_M) exp(−iγ_k H_C) at each layer k = 1, ..., p". So cost unitary exp(−iγ H_C), mixer unitary exp(−iβ H_M).
- Standard mixer: "A common choice of H_M and initial state is −Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} X_i and |+>^{⊗n}". Hence the standard mixer unitary is exp(+iβ Σ X_i), identical to ours.
- Bit/spin map: x_i = (1 − z_i)/2, i.e. z_i = 1 − 2x_i, identical to ours (|0> means x=0, |1> means x=1; "The probability to measure |1> in qubit i is thus c_i*").
- Warm-start mixer: H_{M,i}^(ws) = −sinθ_i X − cosθ_i Z, unitary exp(−iβ H_{M,i}^(ws)) = exp(+iβ(sinθ_i X + cosθ_i Z)); the initial state is its GROUND state (eigenvalue −1).
- Gate definitions: the paper only says R_Y(θ_i) "is a rotation around the Y-axis of qubit i with angle θ_i" and never writes out R_Z. Its statement that R_Y(θ)R_Z(−2β)R_Y(−θ) implements exp(−iβ(−sinθ X − cosθ Z)) holds exactly with the Qiskit definitions RY(t)=exp(−itY/2), RZ(t)=exp(−itZ/2) (checked numerically), so the paper is consistent with Qiskit's definitions.
- MAXCUT: stated as a "max" of the cut (Eq. 6) but solved by minimising an Ising energy: Appendix F's gate diag(1, e^{iγω}, e^{iγω}, 1) equals exp(−iγ (ω/2) Z_iZ_j) up to a global phase, i.e. H_C contains +(ω_ij/2) Z_i Z_j and is minimised. (That last identification is my algebra, not a sentence in the paper.)
- One exception to note: in one place (annealing paragraph of Sec. 3) the text calls the equal-superposition mixer "Σ X_i" without the minus sign; the definition in the introduction and Sec. 2.2 is −Σ X_i.
- Parameter signs: the paper does NOT restrict to γ, β ≥ 0; it samples initial β, γ "uniformly from ±2π" (Sec. 3) and, for p > 1 in Sec. 4, β from [0, 2π] and γ from ±2π.
result.parameters:
CONTINUOUS warm start
- c*: optimum of the convex QP relaxation over [0,1]^n; requires Σ positive semidefinite. In Sec. 3 it is found with IBM ILOG CPLEX 12.10.0.
- ε: allowed range ε in [0, 0.5]. The paper gives NO recommended value for the continuous case; Sec. 3 never mentions ε, and its example has c* ≃ (0.17, 0, 0.97, 0.73, 1.0, 0.14) with exact 0 and 1.0 entries. The Qiskit tutorial uses epsilon=0.0 for that portfolio example. ε = 0.5 reproduces standard QAOA. ε > 0 (or all c_i* in (0,1)) is the condition under which the paper claims convergence to the optimum as p -> infinity.
- Test problem: n = 6 assets, budget B = 3, penalty λ = 3, q = 2, depths p = 1..5, ten runs each; COBYLA with initial β, γ uniform from ±2π; 250 random instances at p = 1.
- Reported result: probability of sampling the optimal bitstring "more than 5 times higher with WS-QAOA then standard QAOA for the simulated depths 1 ≤ p ≤ 5".
- Warm-start initial state with the STANDARD mixer: "the energy of the optimized state does not converge to the minimum energy" - so the warm-start mixer must be used with the warm-start state.

ROUNDED warm start
- ε in (0, 0.5); ε = 0.25 is the value used (yes, 0.25). Two reasons given: (i) with the modified mixer, ε = 0.25, β_1 = π/2, γ_1 = 0 reproduces the GW cut exactly (θ = π/3); (ii) empirical scan in Fig. 7: WS-RQAOA uses "ε = 0.25, chosen based on the results from Fig. 7".
- Fig. 7 numbers (depth 1, ten fully connected 30-node graphs, weights uniform in {−10..10}, five best of ten GW cuts each): median normalised energy 0.907 at ε = 0 (equals the GW cuts), decreasing with ε, starting to rise around ε = 0.15, reaching 0.929 at ε = 0.25.
- Optimiser seeding at depth 1: grid of 25 equally spaced γ_1 from −2π to 2π; for each, energy evaluated at β_1 in {3π/4, 3π/8} and fitted to a sin(2β_1) + b sin(4β_1); best point given to COBYLA.
- WS-RQAOA: N = 10 GW cuts per iteration, best M = 5 unique cuts, p = 1, ε = 0.25, n_stop = n/2; 100 random graphs per type, n = 20 and 30.
- "At ε = 0.25 we often observed that β_1* = π/2 and γ_1* = 0".
- Qiskit reference implementation: WarmStartQAOAOptimizer default epsilon = 0.25; its factory clips x_i to [ε, 1−ε], uses theta = 2*arcsin(sqrt(x_i)), and builds the mixer as ry(-theta), rz(-2*beta), ry(theta) in circuit order - that is the Eq. (2) mixer, NOT the modified rounded mixer.
result.mapping_to_our_convention:
NO SIGN CHANGE IS NEEDED. The paper's convention equals ours: minimise, U_C = exp(−iγ H_C), H_M = −Σ X_i, U_M = exp(−iβ H_M) = exp(+iβ Σ X_i), start |+>^n, z_i = 1 − 2x_i.

RECOMMENDED (continuous / Eq. (2) mixer) - satisfies both requested conditions (a) and (b)

1. Have c_i in [0,1] = relaxed value of bit x_i (probability of measuring 1). If you hold a relaxed spin m_i = <z_i> in [−1,1] instead, c_i = (1 − m_i)/2.
2. Clip: c_i <- min(max(c_i, ε), 1 − ε).
3. θ_i = 2 arcsin(sqrt(c_i)). Then cosθ_i = 1 − 2c_i (= m_i) and sinθ_i = 2 sqrt(c_i(1−c_i)).
4. Initial state per qubit: |φ_i> = RY(θ_i)|0> = sqrt(1−c_i)|0> + sqrt(c_i)|1>. Qiskit: qc.ry(theta_i, i) on |0>. No Hadamard layer.
5. Cost layer unchanged: rzz(2*gamma*J_ij), rz(2*gamma*h_i).
6. Mixer Hamiltonian per qubit: H_M,i = −sinθ_i X − cosθ_i Z = [[2c_i−1, −2sqrt(c_i(1−c_i))],[−2sqrt(c_i(1−c_i)), 1−2c_i]]. |φ_i> is its ground state, eigenvalue −1.
7. Mixer unitary per qubit, as a matrix product with Qiskit gate definitions:
   U_M,i(β) = exp(−iβ H_M,i) = exp(+iβ(sinθ_i X + cosθ_i Z)) = RY(θ_i) · RZ(−2β) · RY(−θ_i)
   Circuit (time) order in Qiskit: qc.ry(-theta_i, i); qc.rz(-2*beta, i); qc.ry(theta_i, i).
   Explicit 2x2 matrix:
   [[ cosβ + i sinβ cosθ_i ,  i sinβ sinθ_i ],
    [ i sinβ sinθ_i ,  cosβ − i sinβ cosθ_i ]]
   and U_M,i(β)|φ_i> = e^{+iβ}|φ_i>.
8. Check (a): initial state is the ground state of H_M with U_M = exp(−iβ H_M). True by construction; verified numerically.
9. Check (b): c_i = 0.5 gives θ_i = π/2, |φ_i> = |+>, H_M,i = −X, and RY(π/2) RZ(−2β) RY(−π/2) = [[cosβ, i sinβ],[i sinβ, cosβ]] = exp(+iβX) = RX(−2β) EXACTLY, with no global phase (numerical difference 2e-16). So ε = 0.5 reproduces our standard QAOA gate for gate.

ROUNDED variant (only if you want the paper's "at least as good as the rounded solution" property)

10. From a rounded bitstring x^r: c_i = ε if x^r_i = 0, c_i = 1 − ε if x^r_i = 1; ε = 0.25 gives θ_i = π/3 or 2π/3. Same initial state as step 4.
11. Modified mixer: U'_i(β) = RY(−θ_i) · RZ(−2β) · RY(θ_i) = exp(−iβ(+sinθ_i X − cosθ_i Z)) = [[cosβ + i sinβ cosθ_i, −i sinβ sinθ_i],[−i sinβ sinθ_i, cosβ − i sinβ cosθ_i]]. Circuit order: qc.ry(theta_i, i); qc.rz(-2*beta, i); qc.ry(-theta_i, i).
12. This mixer does NOT meet conditions (a) or (b): the initial state is not an eigenstate, and at c = 0.5 it becomes exp(−iβX) = RX(+2β), i.e. our standard mixer with β -> −β.
13. At β = π/2, γ = 0, ε = 0.25 it outputs −i|1> where x^r_i = 0 and −i|0> where x^r_i = 1: the BITWISE COMPLEMENT of x^r, with probability 1. That is the same cut for MaxCut (h = 0) but a DIFFERENT energy for our Ising model whenever any h_i ≠ 0.
14. Fix for h ≠ 0 (my derivation, NOT in the paper; checked numerically): build step 10 from the complement of x^r (c_i = 1 − ε where x^r_i = 0, ε where x^r_i = 1). Then β = π/2, γ = 0 returns x^r exactly. Alternative: add one ancilla spin z_0 and replace h_i z_i by h_i z_0 z_i to restore the spin-flip symmetry.

Other implementation notes (my derivations, not paper statements)
- Our Ising model as the paper's QUBO: Σ_ij = 2 J_ij for i ≠ j (symmetric), μ_i = −2(h_i + Σ_{j≠i} J_ij), plus a constant.
- Both warm-start mixers have period π in β up to a global phase, so β in [0, π) is the full range; β = π/2 is inside our β ≥ 0 convention. The usual [0, π/2) reduction of standard QAOA relies on spin-flip symmetry and does not carry over.
result.caveats:
1. The "recover the rounded solution" statement is about the complement. Eq. (3) yields −i|1> for c = ε and −i|0> for c = 1−ε. The paper relies on "z and 1 − z represent the same cut". For an Ising model with fields h_i ≠ 0 this does not hold; see mapping steps 13-14. With the modified mixer and ε = 0.25 the rounded bit itself is never reached with certainty at γ = 0 (max per-qubit probability 0.75, at β = 0).

2. Two different mixers exist in the paper, and they are easy to swap by accident because they differ only in the order of the two RY gates. Continuous: operator RY(θ)RZ(−2β)RY(−θ). Rounded: operator RY(−θ)RZ(−2β)RY(θ). The paper writes operator products (rightmost first); Fig. 2 and Qiskit code are in time order.

3. The rounded mixer costs the convergence argument. Paper: "Since the prepared initial state is no longer an eigenstate of the mixer ... we cannot use the same arguments as in [16] to derive the convergence of the algorithm to the global optimum with increasing depth p." The conclusion calls this "an inconsistency between the mixer and the initial state".

4. The Eq. (2) mixer with a rounded start cannot reproduce the rounded solution: Appendix I, Fig. 14 caption says it "cannot reproduce the GW at ε = 0.25 and depth one", and the energy "does not recover at ε = 0.25". At γ = 0 the state stays the initial product state, so each bit matches the rounded bit with probability 1 − ε only.

5. Convexity. The QP relaxation needs Σ positive semidefinite. An Ising/MaxCut-type Σ with zero diagonal and any non-zero coupling has zero trace and is therefore indefinite (my observation), so the paper's QP route does not apply directly. The paper itself says of MAXCUT: "we cannot relax MAXCUT to a (QP) with a positive semi-definite matrix, without a projection onto the cone of positive-semidefinite matrices" and switches to GW rounding. The paper gives no recipe for convexifying a non-convex QUBO for the continuous route (e.g. diagonal shifting via x_i^2 = x_i is not discussed there).

6. The printed (QP) omits the linear term μ^T x (the paper says μ is added only "when it simplifies the notation"). Over continuous x, x_i^2 ≠ x_i, so the relaxation depends on whether a term is placed on the diagonal or in μ. The portfolio example (Eq. 4) keeps −μ^T x explicitly.

7. Reachability with ε = 0: a qubit with c_i* = 0 or 1 never leaves |0> or |1>. The paper states this for H_C containing only Z_iZ_j and identity terms.

8. Evidence base is small and simulated: 6-asset portfolio instances (statevector), MaxCut graphs of 20 and 30 nodes at depth 1 via an efficient classical simulation, and p > 1 on a single six-node graph. No hardware runs. The paper notes that even at depth one COBYLA from random starts "does not always find the optimal β_1 = π/2 and γ_1 = 0".

9. The "at least as good as GW" guarantee is a statement about the existence of parameters (β = π/2, γ = 0), not about what an optimiser finds, and at those parameters the quantum circuit adds nothing beyond the classical cut.

10. Qiskit's WarmStartQAOAOptimizer always uses the Eq. (2) mixer (default epsilon 0.25), so with a rounded pre-solver it does not implement the paper's modified rounded mixer.

verbatim_quotes: A common choice of ˆHM and initial state is −∑_{i=0}^{n−1} ˆXi and |+⟩^{⊗n}, respectively. Next, in a QAOA with depth p, a quantum circuit applies exp(−iβk ˆHM) exp(−iγk ˆHC) at each layer k = 1, ..., p to create a trial state |ψ(β, γ)⟩.
A classical optimizer seeks the optimal values of β and γ to create a trial state which minimizes the energy of the Hamiltonian ˆHC.

If Σ is positive semidefinite, the trivial continuous relaxation of QUBO min_{x∈[0,1]^n} x^T Σx, (QP) is a convex quadratic program and the optimal solution c∗ of the continuous relaxation is easily obtainable with classical optimizers [64].
If Σ is not positive semidefinite, one can apply the well-known recipe [65] to obtain another continuous-valued relaxation, known as semidefinite programming (SDP)
In QAOA, each decision variable xi of the discrete optimization problem corresponds to a qubit by the relation xi = (1 − zi)/2.

Here, ˆRY (θi) is a rotation around the Y-axis of qubit i with angle θi = 2 arcsin(√c∗i) and c∗i ∈ [0, 1] is the i-th coordinate of the optimum of the continuous-valued relaxation (QP). The probability to measure |1⟩ in qubit i is thus c∗i
and has ˆRY (θi) |0⟩ as ground state with eigenvalue of −1. The ground state of ˆH(ws)M is thus |φ∗⟩ with eigenvalue −n [16].

Since ˆH(ws)M,i = −sin(θi) ˆX − cos(θi) ˆZ the time-evolved mixing Hamiltonian is a rotation around the axis ⃗n = [−sin(θi), 0, −cos(θi)] on the Bloch-sphere of qubit i and can be implemented using the single-qubit rotations ˆRY (θi) ˆRZ(−2β) ˆRY (−θi).

Figure 2: Quantum circuit for WS-QAOA. The first ˆRY rotations prepare the initial state |φ∗⟩. The mixer operator, i.e. ˆRY (θi) ˆRZ(−2βk) ˆRY (−θi), is applied after the time-evolved problem Hamiltonian ˆHC.
In such cases, the qubit will remain in its initial state throughout the QAOA optimization when ˆHC contains only ˆZi ˆZj and identity spin-operators.
we introduce a variant of WS-QAOA that utilizes a regularization parameter ε ∈ [0, 0.5] and changes the rotation angle creating the initial state

The mixer Hamiltonian is adjusted accordingly. The parameter ε provides a continuous mapping between WS-QAOA and standard QAOA since at ε = 0.5 the initial state is the equal superposition state and the mixer Hamiltonian is the X operator.
If all c∗i ∈ (0, 1) or ε > 0, WS-QAOA converges to the optimal solution of (QUBO) as the depth p approaches infinity as does standard QAOA [16].
For a given GW cut we generate an initial state using Y -rotations with a ε ∈ (0, 0.5), as discussed in Sec. 2.2.
We therefore modify the mixer such that its time-evolution is ˆRY (−θi) ˆRZ(−2β) ˆRY (θi) instead of ˆRY (θi) ˆRZ(−2β) ˆRY (−θi), i.e., we multiply the off-diagonal elements in (2) by −1.
With this modification, the value of the regularization parameter ε can be set to 0.25 to generate states that differ from the GW rounding as well as retain it by choosing β1 = π/2 and γ1 = 0.
At these values the depth-one variational form reduces to ˆRY (−θi) ˆRZ(−π) ˆRY (2θi) |0⟩, (3) for each qubit, and creates the states −i |1⟩ and −i |0⟩ when c∗i = ε and 1 − ε, respectively.
Thus, the variational form can recover the solution given by the GW rounding, considering that z and 1 − z represent the same cut

Since the prepared initial state is no longer an eigenstate of the mixer (otherwise we would not be able to deviate from it) we cannot use the same arguments as in [16] to derive the convergence of the algorithm to the global optimum with increasing depth p.

result.formulation:
Read in full: arXiv:2009.10095v4 (LaTeX source main.tex and the PDF, whose footer reads "Accepted in Quantum 2021-06-15"). Equation numbers below are those of v4 / the published PDF. R-gates are written as operator products (rightmost acts first).

SETTING (Sec. 1, 2.1, 2.2)
- (QUBO): min_{x in {0,1}^n} x^T Sigma x + mu^T x, "Sigma in R^{n x n} a symmetric matrix".
- (QP): min_{x in [0,1]^n} x^T Sigma x.
- (SDP): max_{Y in S^n} tr(Sigma Y), diag(Y) = e, Y >= 0 (PSD).
- QAOA layer: exp(-i beta_k H_M) exp(-i gamma_k H_C), k = 1..p. Standard choice H_M = -sum_i X_i with initial state |+>^n. Variable map x_i = (1 - z_i)/2.

1. THETA AND INITIAL STATE
Eq. (1): |phi*> = tensor_{i=0}^{n-1} R_Y(theta_i)|0>_n
with theta_i = 2 arcsin( sqrt(c_i*) ), c_i* in [0,1] the i-th coordinate of the optimum of (QP). "The probability to measure |1> in qubit i is thus c_i*". Circuit (Fig. 2): one R_Y(theta_i) per qubit acting on |0>.

2. WARM-START MIXER
H_M^(ws) = sum_{i=0}^{n-1} H_{M,i}^(ws), with
Eq. (2): H_{M,i}^(ws) = [[ 2c_i* - 1 , -2 sqrt(c_i*(1-c_i*)) ], [ -2 sqrt(c_i*(1-c_i*)) , 1 - 2c_i* ]]
"and has R_Y(theta_i)|0> as ground state with eigenvalue of -1"; ground state of H_M^(ws) is |phi*> with eigenvalue -n. Mixing gate at layer k: exp(-i beta_k H_M^(ws)).
"Since H_{M,i}^(ws) = -sin(theta_i) X - cos(theta_i) Z the time-evolved mixing Hamiltonian is a rotation around the axis n = [-sin(theta_i), 0, -cos(theta_i)] ... and can be implemented using the single-qubit rotations R_Y(theta_i) R_Z(-2 beta) R_Y(-theta_i)."
Sign inside R_Z is NEGATIVE: R_Z(-2 beta) = exp(+i beta Z). Fig. 2 (I rendered the figure and checked it) draws, after the exp(-i gamma_k H_C) block, the gates in TIME order R_Y(-theta_i), R_Z(-2 beta_k), R_Y(theta_i), which is the same operator product.

3. REGULARISATION AND ROUNDED WARM START
Unnumbered display between Eq. (2) and Eq. (3), epsilon in [0, 0.5]:
 theta_i = 2 arcsin(sqrt(c_i*)) if c_i* in [epsilon, 1-epsilon];
 theta_i = 2 arcsin(sqrt(epsilon)) if c_i* <= epsilon;
 theta_i = 2 arcsin(sqrt(1-epsilon)) if c_i* >= 1-epsilon.
"The mixer Hamiltonian is adjusted accordingly." At epsilon = 0.5 "the initial state is the equal superposition state and the mixer Hamiltonian is the X operator".
Rounded case (Sec. 2.3): initial state built from a GW cut "using Y-rotations with a epsilon in (0, 0.5)". The mixer is MODIFIED: "its time-evolution is R_Y(-theta_i) R_Z(-2 beta) R_Y(theta_i) instead of R_Y(theta_i) R_Z(-2 beta) R_Y(-theta_i), i.e., we multiply the off-diagonal elements in (2) by -1".
"the value of the regularization parameter epsilon can be set to 0.25 to generate states that differ from the GW rounding as well as retain it by choosing beta_1 = pi/2 and gamma_1 = 0." At these values the depth-one variational form reduces to
Eq. (3): R_Y(-theta_i) R_Z(-pi) R_Y(2 theta_i) |0>
"for each qubit, and creates the states -i|1> and -i|0> when c_i* = epsilon and 1-epsilon, respectively." So every bit is FLIPPED; the GW cut is recovered only "considering that z and 1 - z represent the same cut". "Therefore, WS-QAOA is at least as good as GW rounding."
Eigenstate property of the rounded-case mixer: NO. "Since the prepared initial state is no longer an eigenstate of the mixer (otherwise we would not be able to deviate from it) we cannot use the same arguments as in [16] to derive the convergence of the algorithm to the global optimum with increasing depth p." The conclusion repeats this as "an inconsistency between the mixer and the initial state". With the unmodified Eq. (2) mixer the paper says (Fig. 14 caption) it "cannot reproduce the GW at epsilon=0.25 and depth one".

4. CONVEX QP CONDITION
"If Sigma is positive semidefinite, the trivial continuous relaxation of QUBO [(QP)] is a convex quadratic program and the optimal solution c* of the continuous relaxation is easily obtainable with classical optimizers". "If Sigma is not positive semidefinite, one can apply the well-known recipe ... semidefinite programming (SDP)". For MAXCUT: "Since we cannot relax MAXCUT to a (QP) with a positive semi-definite matrix, without a projection onto the cone of positive-semidefinite matrices, we now warm-start QAOA with a binary solution obtained using the GW rounding."

MAXCUT OBJECTIVE AND COST GATE
Eq. (6): max (1/2) sum_{(i,j) in E} omega_ij (1 - z_i z_j), z in {-1,1}^{|V|}. Appendix F gives the edge gate U_{i,j} = diag(1, e^{i gamma omega_ij}, e^{i gamma omega_ij}, 1), which equals exp(-i gamma (omega_ij/2) Z_i Z_j) up to a global phase.
result.sign_conventions:
PAPER
- MINIMISES. "A classical optimizer seeks the optimal values of beta and gamma to create a trial state which minimizes the energy of the Hamiltonian H_C"; H_C is a Hamiltonian "whose ground state is the optimum solution".
- Layer exp(-i beta_k H_M) exp(-i gamma_k H_C); standard H_M = -sum_i X_i, so the standard mixer unitary is exp(+i beta sum X). Initial state is the GROUND state of the mixer.
- x_i = (1 - z_i)/2, i.e. z = 1 - 2x: |0> means x = 0, |1> means x = 1.
- This is IDENTICAL to our convention. No sign change is needed for cost unitary, mixer or bit mapping.
- MAXCUT is stated as a maximisation (Eq. 6) but is run as energy minimisation ("minimizing the energy of depth-one WS-QAOAs"). Appendix F's edge gate corresponds to H_C = +(1/2) sum_{i<j} omega_ij Z_i Z_j up to a constant, evolved as exp(-i gamma H_C), i.e. J_ij = omega_ij/2 in our notation. Appendix G's Eq. (24) writes the "MAXCUT Hamiltonian" as (1/4) sum_{i,j} omega_ij (1 - Z_i Z_j), which is the cut value, not the minimised operator.
- R_Y, R_Z are never defined explicitly. The Qiskit definitions RY(t)=exp(-i t Y/2), RZ(t)=exp(-i t Z/2) are the only ones consistent with all three of: P(|1>) = c_i*, Eq. (2) matching the stated decomposition, and the exact phases -i|1>, -i|0> of Eq. (3). I confirmed all three numerically.
- Two inconsistencies inside the paper: (a) the annealing paragraph of Sec. 3 calls the standard mixer "sum_i X_i" without the minus sign, and Sec. 2.2 says "the mixer Hamiltonian is the X operator" at epsilon = 0.5, whereas Eq. (2) at c = 0.5 gives -X; (b) Algorithm 1 writes the two-qubit mixer as exp(-i beta (H_{M,i} tensor H_{M,j})), a leftover from v1 where H_M^(ws) was a tensor product; the main text of v4 uses a sum.

QISKIT (source read on main and stable/0.6; docs 0.7.0)
- create_initial_state: theta = 2*np.arcsin(np.sqrt(relaxed_value)); circuit.ry(theta, index). Matches Eq. (1).
- create_mixer, docstring "Creates an evolved mixer circuit as Ry(theta)Rz(-2beta)Ry(-theta)", code in time order: circuit.ry(-theta, index); circuit.rz(-2.0 * beta, index); circuit.ry(theta, index). This is the operator RY(theta) RZ(-2beta) RY(-theta) = exp(-i beta H_ws) of Eq. (2), the EIGENSTATE mixer. It matches the paper's continuous warm start.
- Qiskit does NOT implement the modified Sec. 2.3 mixer. With a rounded pre-solver and the default factory you get the Eq. (2) mixer, which the paper says cannot reproduce the GW cut at depth one.
- create_initial_variables clips to [epsilon, 1-epsilon] (default epsilon = 0.25), matching the paper's rule. The docstring line "xi = 1-epsilon if xi > epsilon" is a typo; the code tests variable > 1.0 - epsilon.
- QAOAAnsatz appends a circuit-type mixer as-is and evolves the cost with PauliEvolutionGate(op, gamma) = exp(-i gamma H_C); to_ising uses x_i = (1 - Z_i)/2 on a minimisation QUBO. The full Qiskit warm-start layer is therefore exp(-i beta H_ws) exp(-i gamma H_C), identical to the paper and to ours.
- Qiskit's DEFAULT QAOAAnsatz mixer is +sum X evolved as exp(-i beta sum X) = RX(+2 beta), the opposite sign to the paper and to us. So Qiskit warm-start at epsilon = 0.5 equals Qiskit's own standard QAOA only after beta -> -beta.

FROM THE PAPER

- p > 1 study: one six-node graph (maximum cut 27, initial cut 001111 of size 23), 30 runs, beta uniform in [0, 2pi], gamma in +-2pi, p = 1..6.
- Portfolio (continuous warm start, Eq. (2) mixer): n = 6, q = 2, B = 3, penalty lambda = 3, p = 1..5, COBYLA, ten runs with (beta, gamma) uniform in +-2pi, c* from CPLEX 12.10.0; 250 random instances at p = 1. Replacing the warm-start mixer by the standard one while keeping the warm initial state "does not converge to the minimum energy".
- The paper does not restrict beta, gamma to be non-negative.

FROM QISKIT

MEASURED BY ME (not in the paper; script paths under mapping)
- Modified mixer at beta = pi/2, gamma = 0: per-qubit flip probability is 0.392, 0.676, 0.864, 0.968, 1.000, 0.972, 0.784, 0.500 for epsilon = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50. On that grid, 0.25 is the only value giving a deterministic basis state.
- Variance of the modified mixer Hamiltonian in the initial state at epsilon = 0.25 is 0.75 (expectation +0.5). It is zero only at c = 0, 0.5, 1.
- Eq. (2) mixer at gamma = 0: output distribution equals the initial product distribution for every beta, so P(rounded bitstring) = (1-epsilon)^n: 0.2373 for n = 5, and 0.75^30 = 1.79e-4 for n = 30.
result.mapping_to_our_convention:
The paper's convention equals ours (minimise; exp(-i gamma H); mixer exp(-i beta H_M) with the initial state as ground state; z = 1 - 2x). Use the paper's gates unchanged, with beta >= 0.

STEP BY STEP
1. Take c_i in [0,1] (relaxation optimum, or c_i = x_i for a rounded bitstring). Clip to [eps, 1-eps].
2. theta_i = 2*arcsin(sqrt(c_i)). Initial state: qc.ry(theta_i, i) on |0>, giving sqrt(1-c_i)|0> + sqrt(c_i)|1>, so P(x_i=1) = c_i.
3. Cost layer unchanged: rzz(2*gamma*J_ij) and rz(2*gamma*h_i).
4. Mixer A (continuous warm start, Eq. 2; initial state IS the ground state; this is what Qiskit implements). Per qubit, in TIME order: qc.ry(-theta_i, i); qc.rz(-2*beta, i); qc.ry(theta_i, i). Equals exp(+i beta (sin(theta_i) X + cos(theta_i) Z)). For c_i = 0.5 it equals rx(-2*beta) = exp(+i beta X), our standard mixer.
5. Mixer B (rounded warm start, Sec. 2.3; initial state is NOT an eigenstate). Per qubit, in TIME order: qc.ry(theta_i, i); qc.rz(-2*beta, i); qc.ry(-theta_i, i). Equals exp(+i beta (cos(theta_i) Z - sin(theta_i) X)). For c_i = 0.5 it equals rx(+2*beta) = exp(-i beta X), the INVERSE of our standard mixer. With eps = 0.25, (beta, gamma) = (pi/2, 0) flips every qubit deterministically.
The main trap: the paper's R_Y(theta) R_Z(-2beta) R_Y(-theta) is an operator product, so the first gate in the circuit is ry(-theta). Reversing the order silently swaps Mixer A for Mixer B.

WHICH MIXER FOR OUR PROBLEM (we have fields h_i)
- Mixer B at (pi/2, 0) returns the bitwise COMPLEMENT of the rounded solution. That is the same solution only if E(z) = E(-z), i.e. all h_i = 0. With fields, the paper's "at least as good as the rounded solution" guarantee does not transfer as written. In my test, a 5-spin instance with fields gave E(rounded) = +1.0313 against E(complement) = +2.3946.
- Options, none of them from the paper: (i) use Mixer A with eps > 0, accepting that depth one cannot reproduce the rounded bitstring with certainty; (ii) build both the initial state and Mixer B from the complemented bitstring (c -> 1-c), so that (pi/2, 0) returns the intended bitstring with probability 1 (verified numerically); (iii) add one ancilla spin z_0 and replace h_i z_i by h_i z_0 z_i to restore the Z2 symmetry (standard trick, not tested here).
- Restricting gamma >= 0 loses nothing if beta spans a full period [0, pi): all matrices are real, so <E>(gamma, beta) = <E>(-gamma, pi - beta), and beta has period pi. Verified numerically for the standard mixer, A and B. Do not reuse a beta range tuned for the standard mixer with Mixer B: at eps = 0.5, B is the standard mixer with beta -> -beta.

CONVEX RELAXATION FOR OUR ISING FORM (my derivation, checked by enumeration to 4e-15)
With z = 1 - 2x: E = x^T S x + m^T x + const, S_ij = S_ji = 2 J_ij (i != j), S_ii = 0, m_i = -2 (sum_{j != i} J_ij + h_i), const = sum_{i<j} J_ij + sum_i h_i. S has zero trace, so it is never PSD unless J = 0. Since x_i^2 = x_i on binaries, replace S by S + d*I and m by m - d with d >= -lambda_min(S) to get a convex QP. c* then depends on d; the paper does not discuss this choice.

result.caveats:
1. VERSION TRAP, the likeliest source of disagreement between two readers. arXiv v1 (Sep 2020) states a single mixer, written R_Y(-theta_i) R_Z(-2 beta) R_Y(theta_i), for everything, and has no sentence about the eigenstate property. From v2 onward (and in the published v4) the eigenstate mixer is R_Y(theta_i) R_Z(-2 beta) R_Y(-theta_i) and the reversed order is introduced explicitly as the modified mixer for the rounded case. I checked the LaTeX of v1, v2, v3 and v4. Anyone reading v1 will report the opposite gate order for the continuous case.

2. Operator order versus circuit order. The paper's products act right to left; Fig. 2 and Qiskit list gates in time order. The same mixer therefore appears as "R_Y(theta) R_Z(-2beta) R_Y(-theta)" in the text and as ry(-theta), rz(-2beta), ry(theta) in code.

3. The rounded-case recovery returns the complement of the rounded bitstring, not the bitstring itself. The paper relies on MAXCUT's symmetry ("z and 1 - z represent the same cut"). For our Ising energy with fields this is a different, generally worse, solution. See the mapping for workarounds, which are mine and not the paper's.

4. The modified mixer has the initial state as a non-eigenstate, so the paper's adiabatic convergence argument does not apply to it; the paper says so and only studies it numerically. The exact retention at beta = pi/2 is specific to epsilon = 0.25 in my scan.

5. Qiskit's WarmStartQAOAOptimizer matches the paper's continuous warm start (Eq. 1 initial state, Eq. 2 mixer, epsilon clipping) but not the rounded-case mixer of Sec. 2.3. To reproduce Sec. 2.3 one must supply a custom warm_start_factory whose create_mixer emits ry(theta), rz(-2beta), ry(-theta). Qiskit's _relax_problem only switches variables to continuous; it does not check or enforce convexity.

6. Qiskit's default (non-warm-start) QAOAAnsatz mixer has the opposite sign to the paper and to our convention (verified: overlap 1.000 with exp(-i beta sum X), 0.342 with exp(+i beta sum X) on a test instance).

7. With epsilon = 0 and c_i in {0,1} the qubit never leaves its initial state when H_C contains only ZZ and identity terms (paper, Sec. 2.2). The convergence statement needs "all c_i* in (0,1) or epsilon > 0".

8. The paper's convex-QP statement is for min x^T Sigma x with mu absorbed into the diagonal. The diagonal-shift convexification and the Ising-to-QUBO coefficients in the mapping are my own derivation, numerically checked, not statements from the paper.

9. Items labelled as measured by me or as my derivation (flip-probability table, Z2 workarounds, the gamma/beta symmetry) are not claims of the paper.

CITATION CHECK: the believed reference is correct exactly as given. Title "Improving Variational Quantum Optimization using CVaR"; authors in order Panagiotis Kl. Barkoutsos, Giacomo Nannicini, Anton Robert, Ivano Tavernelli, Stefan Woerner; Quantum 4, 256 (2020); DOI 10.22331/q-2020-04-20-256 (Crossref: volume 4, article 256, issued 2020-04-20); arXiv:1907.04769. Confirmed on the arXiv abstract page, the Quantum journal page and Crossref.

EQUATIONS (arXiv v3 PDF, equation numbers as printed):
(1) min_theta <psi(theta)| H |psi(theta)>   -- the standard objective.
(2) min_{x in {0,1}^n} b^T x + x^T A x   (QUBO).
(3) min_{z in {-1,+1}^n} c^T z + z^T Q z   (Ising), with "the variable transformation x_i = (1 - z_i)/2".
(4) sigma_Z = diag(1, -1); z_i -> sigma_Z^i, z_i z_j -> sigma_Z^i (x) sigma_Z^j.
(5) sample mean (1/K) sum_{k=1}^{K} H_k(theta), where H_k are the K sampled energies.
(6) U_C(gamma) = exp( -i gamma ( sum_{i=1}^n c_i sigma_Z^i + sum_{i,j=1}^n Q_ij sigma_Z^i (x) sigma_Z^j ) ).
(7) U_B(beta) = exp( -i beta sum_{i=1}^n sigma_X^i ).
(9) U(beta, gamma) = [ prod_{i=1}^p U_B(beta_i) U_C(gamma_i) ] H^{(x) n}  (H here = Hadamard), with beta, gamma in R^p.
(10) |psi(beta,gamma)> = U(beta,gamma)|0>.
(11) CVaR_alpha(X) = E[ X | X <= F_X^{-1}(alpha) ],  alpha in (0,1], F_X the CDF of X: "the expected value of the lower alpha-tail of the distribution of X".
(12) sample version, samples sorted in nondecreasing order (H_{k+1} >= H_k), for {H_k}_{k=1..K}:
     (1/ceil(alpha K)) * sum_{k=0}^{ceil(alpha K)} H_k.
     NOTE: the lower summation limit is printed as k=0 in the PDF (checked on a rendered image of page 4, and the arXiv HTML shows the same), although the samples are indexed k=1..K. Read literally that is ceil(alpha K)+1 terms with an undefined H_0; it is almost certainly an index typo for k=1. The intended estimator is the mean of the ceil(alpha K) lowest sampled energies.
(13) min_theta CVaR_alpha(X(theta)), where X(theta) takes value H_{j,j} with probability |alpha_j(theta)|^2.
Appendix A: "we can apply RX(-2 beta) to each qubit to implement U_B"; Fig. 7: CNOT - RZ(-2 gamma) on target - CNOT as "Implementation of e^{-i gamma sigma_Z^i (x) sigma_Z^j} up to a global phase".
Appendix D: mixer matrix entries "a00 = a11 = cos beta, a01 = a10 = -i sin beta" (i.e. e^{-i beta X}, consistent with Eq. 7).

AUTHORS' REFERENCE CODE (notebook compute_cvar(probabilities, values, alpha)): sort values ascending, accumulate probability until the total reaches alpha, giving the boundary outcome the weight (alpha - total_prob), then divide by total_prob. qiskit-algorithms _get_cvar_aggregation does the same and returns cvar / alpha. For alpha*K integer this equals the mean of the alpha*K lowest shots; for non-integer alpha*K it is a fractional-boundary variant that differs slightly from the ceil form of Eq. (12).
result.sign_conventions:
MINIMISE or MAXIMISE: the paper MINIMISES. Eq. (1), (2), (3) and (13) are all "min", CVaR is the LOWER alpha-tail, samples are sorted in nondecreasing order, and the returned solution is the bitstring with the smallest H_k. This is the same direction as our convention, so the CVaR objective needs no sign flip.

BIT/SPIN MAP: paper uses x_i = (1 - z_i)/2 and sigma_Z = diag(1,-1), i.e. |0> <-> z=+1 <-> x=0 and |1> <-> z=-1 <-> x=1. Identical to ours (z_i = 1 - 2 x_i).

ISING FORM: paper writes c^T z + z^T Q z with a full double sum over i,j=1..n. Ours is sum_{i<j} J_ij z_i z_j + sum_i h_i z_i + const, so h_i = c_i, J_ij = Q_ij + Q_ji for i<j, and the diagonal Q_ii go into the constant (z_i^2 = 1).

COST UNITARY: paper Eq. (6) U_C(gamma) = exp(-i gamma H). Same sign as ours.

MIXER UNITARY: paper Eq. (7) U_B(beta) = exp(-i beta sum X). OPPOSITE sign in the exponent to our U_M(beta) = exp(+i beta sum X). So beta_ours = -beta_paper when using Eq. (6)-(7). The paper places no sign restriction on the angles (beta, gamma in R^p), and gives no recommended angle values, so nothing numerical has to be transported.

START STATE: Hadamard layer on |0>^n, i.e. |+>^n. Same as ours. Layer order U_B U_C (cost first, then mixer). Same as ours.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER (harmless): with Qiskit's definitions RX(t)=exp(-i t X/2), RZ(t)=exp(-i t Z/2), Appendix A's RX(-2 beta) equals exp(+i beta X) and Fig. 7's CNOT.RZ(-2 gamma).CNOT equals exp(+i gamma ZZ). Both are the opposite sign to Eq. (6)-(7). Flipping both signs complex-conjugates the whole circuit (H and X are real, |+>^n is real), so measurement probabilities are identical. I checked all of this numerically with explicit matrices and a 10-qubit random Ising QAOA: max |p_Eq(6,7) - p_AppendixA| = 0.0; max |p_ours(gamma,beta) - p_Eq(6,7)(gamma,-beta)| = 0.0; max |p_ours(gamma,beta) - p_Eq(6,7)(gamma,beta)| = 0.026 (so the sign does matter if angles are copied without the flip). Note Appendix A's mixer gate RX(-2 beta) is literally our rx(-2*beta), while its cost gate (equivalent to rzz(-2 gamma)) is the opposite of our rzz(2*gamma*J_ij).

The CVaR aggregation itself is classical post-processing of sampled energies and is independent of all unitary sign conventions.
result.parameters:
ALPHA VALUES STUDIED: simulation: alpha in {1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%} (alpha = 100% is the ordinary expectation value). Hardware: alpha = 10%, 25%, 100%.

ALPHA RECOMMENDED: "Results in this paper suggest choosing alpha in [0.1, 0.25] as a good empirical choice". Elsewhere the paper says the benefits are obvious for alpha in [0.01, 0.25]. It also states alpha "can be chosen as a constant, independent of the number of qubits". Our alpha = 0.1 sits at the lower end of the recommended range.

CLASSICAL OPTIMISER: COBYLA, for both simulation and hardware ("Following [17], we use the classical optimizer COBYLA"). The paper text gives no COBYLA hyperparameters. The authors' notebook uses COBYLA(maxiter=100) with initial_point = np.random.rand(m); on hardware the paper fixes the initial parameters to theta = 0.

APPLIED TO: BOTH in simulation. CVaR-VQE with RY + CZ (all-to-all) ansatz at p = 0, 1, 2 and CVaR-QAOA at p = 1, 2, 3. On hardware ONLY CVaR-VQE was run (IBM Q Poughkeepsie, 6 qubits, portfolio optimisation, p = 0, 1, 2, nearest-neighbour ring entanglement, 5 repeats); CVaR-QAOA was not run on hardware.

TEST SET: six problem classes (maximum stable set, Max-3-SAT, number partitioning, MaxCut, market split, portfolio optimisation); ten random instances each at 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 qubits (Max-3-SAT at 6, 9, 12, 15); 340 instances and 14,280 test cases in total (I checked the arithmetic: 340 x 7 alphas x 6 ansatz/depth settings = 14,280).

SHOTS: simulation results use "the exact quantum state resulting from simulation" (no shot noise; no shot count given). Hardware: 8,192 samples per trial wavefunction, the same number for every alpha.

SHOT RULE OF THUMB FROM THE PAPER: to match the accuracy of the expectation value, increase samples by a factor 1/alpha, i.e. a factor in [4, 10] for alpha in [0.1, 0.25]. For our alpha = 0.1 that means 10,000 shots to match a 1,000-shot mean; with 1,000 shots the estimator rests on 100 shots.

PERFORMANCE METRIC USED BY THE PAPER: probability of sampling an optimal solution (ground-state overlap), as the fraction of instances reaching >= 1% and >= 10%, plotted against iterations normalised by the number of qubits (up to 50 normalised iterations).
result.mapping_to_our_convention:
The paper minimises, as we do, with the same bit/spin map, the same start state and the same cost-unitary sign. Only the mixer exponent sign differs (beta_ours = -beta_paper for Eq. 7), and that does not touch the CVaR estimator. Nothing in our circuit changes; only the scalar handed to the classical optimiser changes.

ESTIMATOR TO CODE (alpha = 0.1, K = 1000 shots):
1. Run our usual circuit (|+>^n, then per layer rzz(2*gamma*J_ij), rz(2*gamma*h_i), rx(-2*beta)) and measure K = 1000 shots.
2. Convert EVERY shot to an energy with our formula E(z) = sum_{i<j} J_ij z_i z_j + sum_i h_i z_i + const, z_i = 1 - 2 x_i. Qiskit count keys are little-endian (qubit 0 is the rightmost character); the authors' notebook reverses the string for this reason. Expand counts so there is one energy per shot (1000 values), or equivalently weight by counts.
3. Sort the 1000 energies ascending (lowest = best, because we minimise).
4. m = ceil(alpha*K) = ceil(0.1*1000) = 100.
5. CVaR_0.1 = (1/100) * (sum of the 100 lowest energies) = mean of E_sorted[0:100]. Return this to the optimiser to MINIMISE.

    def cvar(energies, alpha):
        e = np.sort(np.asarray(energies, dtype=float))   # ascending, one entry per shot
        m = int(np.ceil(alpha * e.size - 1e-9))          # alpha=0.1, K=1000 -> 100
        return e[:m].mean()

Implementation notes (checked numerically, script at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-t/7c811c50-f516-4e09-a51a-78bd3f6d1c7e/scratchpad/cvar_lit/check_cvar.py):
- Treat Eq. (12)'s printed lower limit k=0 as a typo; use the ceil(alpha K) lowest samples (k = 1..ceil(alpha K)).
- In Python 0.1*1000 == 100.0 exactly, so ceil gives 100. The small -1e-9 guard matters for other values (0.07*100 evaluates to 7.000000000000001, so a bare ceil gives 8).
- For alpha = 0.1, K = 1000, this estimator agrees to 10 decimals with the authors' notebook compute_cvar and with qiskit-algorithms' CVaR aggregation applied to the empirical frequencies. They differ only when alpha*K is not an integer (e.g. K = 1024: -25.189 for the ceil form vs -25.215 for the fractional-boundary form on my test state), so with 1000 shots there is no ambiguity.
- Do not deduplicate bitstrings before taking the lowest 10%: the tail is 10% of SHOTS (probability mass), not 10% of distinct bitstrings.
- alpha = 1 must reproduce the plain sample mean; use that as a unit test.
- If an exact statevector is used instead of shots, use the probability-weighted form: sort energies ascending, accumulate probability to alpha with fractional weight on the boundary state, divide by alpha.
- Angles: our gamma, beta >= 0 with U_M = exp(+i beta sum X) corresponds to (gamma, -beta) in the paper's Eq. (6)-(7). The paper leaves angles unconstrained in R^p and optimises with COBYLA, so if you follow the paper's optimiser setup there is no bound to translate; if you keep our gamma, beta >= 0 bounds that is our choice, not the paper's.

WHAT MUST STILL BE REPORTED FOR A FAIR COMPARISON WITH ORDINARY QAOA:
The CVaR_0.1 value is not an expectation value and must never be set side by side with ordinary QAOA's <H>. The paper says so directly ("the reported objective function values for different values of alpha are incomparable") and compares methods on an alpha-independent metric. Report, for both the CVaR-trained and the expectation-trained circuit, evaluated at the final parameters:
(a) the plain expectation value <H> = mean of ALL K shots (the alpha = 1 aggregate), ideally also the exact statevector value;
(b) the probability of sampling the optimal solution (ground-state overlap), which is the paper's own cross-alpha metric, when the optimum is known;
(c) the best sampled energy min_k H_k and the corresponding bitstring (this is what the paper's algorithm returns), or the approximation ratio derived from it;
(d) the same shot budget, same number of objective evaluations/iterations, same depth p and same initial point for both objectives (the paper normalises iterations by the number of qubits).
Optionally also evaluate both circuits under the same CVaR_0.1 on fresh shots, but (a) to (c) are the comparable quantities.
result.caveats:
Caveats stated in the paper:
1. The objective is no longer the expectation value and the landscapes do not map onto each other: Proposition 5.1, "A local minimum of (1) does not necessarily correspond to a local minimum of (13), and vice versa"; global minima cannot be mapped either, except when the ansatz can reach the ground state of a diagonal H.
2. Soft cap at alpha: "the value of alpha introduces a soft cap on the maximum probability of sampling a ground state"; "the CVaR objective function does not provide any incentive to increase the overlap with the optimal solution beyond alpha". With alpha = 0.1, expect the ground-state probability to plateau around 10%; with alpha = 1% only a small fraction of instances reached 10%. On hardware at p = 2 and alpha = 25% the probability plateaued slightly below alpha.
3. Shots: the estimator uses only a subset of the measurements; stated variance O(1/(K alpha^2)), rule "increase the number of samples to K/alpha". The paper's own experiments nevertheless held shots fixed across alpha and argue a noisy CVaR estimate still guided the optimiser better.
4. QAOA benefits less than VQE: "QAOA's performance appears significantly worse than that of VQE for equivalent depth"; for CVaR-QAOA improvement is reported "as p increases and alpha decreases (up to a certain level)". Proposition 7.1 argues fixed-small-p QAOA gives "flat" states with small overlap. Hardware used CVaR-VQE "because for the same circuit depth it leads to better solutions".
5. No claim of competitiveness with classical heuristics ("we do not claim that this brings their performance on par with state-of-the-art classical heuristics"). Sizes are 6 to 16 qubits.

My own observations (not statements from the paper):
6. Eq. (12) prints the sum from k=0; samples are indexed from 1. Treat as a typo.
7. The shot-count argument is internally loose: a variance of O(1/(K alpha^2)) taken literally would call for K/alpha^2 samples, yet the paper says K/alpha (factor 4 to 10). Treat 1/alpha as a rule of thumb. I did not read reference [13] to settle it.
8. From a visual reading of Fig. 4, the QAOA curves for the different alpha values lie almost on top of each other (roughly 0.55 to 0.62 of instances reaching 1% overlap, 0.15 to 0.28 reaching 10%), in contrast to the wide spread for VQE. The evidence in this paper for CVaR helping QAOA specifically is therefore modest; do not promise a large gain in the notebook.
9. The paper never tests shot-based CVaR-QAOA: QAOA results are exact-state simulations only, and the hardware runs are VQE with 8,192 shots. Our setting (QAOA, 1000 shots, alpha = 0.1, so 100 tail shots) is outside what the paper measured.
10. One toy check of estimator noise (single 10-qubit random-Ising p=2 QAOA state at arbitrary angles, 4000 repetitions; illustrative only, not a general result): standard error of the 1000-shot mean 0.298 vs 0.459 for the 1000-shot CVaR_0.1 (ratio 1.5, well below the factor implied by 1/alpha), finite-sample bias of CVaR_0.1 +0.029 at K = 1000 and consistent with zero at K = 10,000 (energy scale: mean -8.8, minimum -28.5).
11. Eq. (6)-(7) and Appendix A use opposite signs for both unitaries; this is a global complex conjugation and has no effect on outcomes (see sign_conventions).

verbatim_quotes: Formally, the CVaR of a random variable X for a confidence level alpha in (0, 1] is defined as CVaR_alpha(X) = E[X | X <= F_X^{-1}(alpha)] (11) where F_X denotes the cumulative density function of X. In other words, CVaR is the expected value of the lower alpha-tail of the distribution of X.

Without loss of generality, assume that the samples H_k are sorted in nondecreasing order, i.e. H_{k+1} >= H_k. Then, for a given set of samples {H_k}_{k=1,...,K} and value of alpha, the CVaR_alpha is defined as (1/ceil(alpha K)) sum_{k=0}^{ceil(alpha K)} H_k. (12)
Note that the limit alpha -> 0 corresponds to the minimum, and alpha = 1 corresponds to the expected value of X.

It is clear that this can be applied to both VQE and QAOA, simply by replacing the sample mean (5) with CVaR_alpha in the classical optimization algorithm. We call the resulting algorithms CVaR-VQE and CVaR-QAOA, respectively.
For every instance, we run CVaR-VQE and CVaR-QAOA for alpha in {1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%} and p = 0, 1, 2 for VQE and p = 1, 2, 3 for QAOA.
Following [17], we use the classical optimizer COBYLA to determine the parameters of the trial wave function.

=== (A) LR-QAOA (equation numbers are arXiv v3; the npj version has the same equations numbered one higher: (2),(3),(4),(5) and (13)) ===
Cost Hamiltonian, Eq. (1): H_C = sum_i h_i sigma_z^i + sum_{i,j>i} J_ij sigma_z^i sigma_z^j
Cost unitary, Eq. (2): U_C(H_C, gamma_i) = e^{-j gamma_i H_C}
Mixer unitary, Eq. (3): U(H_B, beta_i) = e^{j beta_i H_B}, with H_B = sum_{i=0}^{N_q-1} sigma_i^x, and the paper states R_X(-2 beta_i) = e^{j beta_i sigma^x}
Initial state: |+>^{(x) N_q}
Linear ramp, Eq. (4): beta_i = (1 - i/p) Delta_beta and gamma_i = ((i+1)/p) Delta_gamma, for i = 0,...,p-1
  Endpoints: beta_0 = Delta_beta, beta_{p-1} = Delta_beta/p (never reaches 0); gamma_0 = Delta_gamma/p, gamma_{p-1} = Delta_gamma.
  Layer order: cost unitary first, then the mixer ("in every second part of a layer").
Normalisation, Eq. (12): H_c(z) = (1/max{|J_ij|}) ( sum_{i=0}^{n-1} sum_{j>i}^{n-1} J_ij z_i z_j + sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h_i z_i + O ), where the offset O is dropped. The paper normalises by max{|J_ij|} for almost all cases, and by max{|h_i|} for MIS; the alternative they tested is max{|h_i, J_ij|}.
Related, Eq. (6)-(7): alpha_k^{t+1} = e^{j theta_k^t} alpha_k^t, theta_k^t = E_k gamma_t, with E_k = <k|H_c|k> (see caveats: sign inconsistent with Eq. (2)).
Mixer action, Eq. (8): alpha_k^{t+1} = sum_l (cos beta_t)^{N_q - k.l} (j sin beta_t)^{k.l} alpha_l^t, k.l = Hamming distance.

=== (B) SPSA (Spall 1998, Section III.A, steps 1-5; transcribed from the scanned pages) ===
Step 1: counter k = 0; gain sequences a_k = a/(A + k + 1)^alpha and c_k = c/(k + 1)^gamma. "Practically effective (and theoretically valid) values for alpha and gamma are 0.602 and 0.101, respectively (the asymptotically optimal values of 1.0 and 1/6 may also be used)".
Step 2: perturbation vector Delta_k, each of the p components drawn independently from a Bernoulli +-1 distribution with probability 1/2 for each outcome (uniform and normal are not allowed: infinite inverse moments).
Step 3: two loss measurements y(theta_k + c_k Delta_k) and y(theta_k - c_k Delta_k), where y(theta) = L(theta) + noise.
Step 4: g_hat_k(theta_k) = [ y(theta_k + c_k Delta_k) - y(theta_k - c_k Delta_k) ] / (2 c_k) * [Delta_k1^{-1}, Delta_k2^{-1}, ..., Delta_kp^{-1}]^T
Step 5: theta_{k+1} = theta_k - a_k g_hat_k(theta_k)
Appendix MATLAB (Fig. 1), loop "For k=1:n": ak=a/(k+A)^alpha; ck=c/k^gamma; delta=2*round(rand(p,1))-1; thetaplus=theta+ck*delta; thetaminus=theta-ck*delta; yplus=loss(thetaplus); yminus=loss(thetaminus); ghat=(yplus-yminus)./(2*ck*delta); theta=theta-ak*ghat;
Spall 1992: Eq. (2.1) theta_{k+1} = theta_k - a_k g_hat_k(theta_k); measurements y_k^(+-) = L(theta_k +- c_k Delta_k) + eps_k^(+-); Eq. (2.2) g_hat_k(theta_k) = [ (y_k^(+) - y_k^(-))/(2 c_k Delta_k1), ..., (y_k^(+) - y_k^(-))/(2 c_k Delta_kp) ]^T; Eq. (2.3) optional average of q independent estimates. Assumption A1: a_k, c_k > 0, a_k -> 0, c_k -> 0, sum a_k = infinity, sum (a_k/c_k)^2 < infinity. Proposition 2 uses a_k = a/k^alpha, c_k = c/k^gamma with beta = alpha - 2 gamma > 0 and 3 gamma - alpha/2 >= 0.

=== (C) Lucas, Section 2.2 Graph Partitioning (identical in arXiv v3 and the Frontiers PDF) ===
Eq. (7): H = H_A + H_B
Eq. (8): H_A = A ( sum_{n=1}^{N} s_i )^2   [index printed as n with summand s_i in both versions]
Eq. (9): H_B = B sum_{(uv) in E} (1 - s_u s_v)/2
Eq. (10): A/B >= min(2 Delta, N)/8, where Delta is the maximal degree of G
Spins s_v = +-1 on each vertex; N = |V| even; goal: two subsets of equal size N/2 with the number of connecting edges minimised. Eq. (11) is the constraint form of the original reference, sum_{i=1}^{N} s_i = 0, which Lucas replaces by the penalty H_A. Eq. (12) defines Lucas's bit variable x_alpha = (s_alpha + 1)/2.
result.sign_conventions:
=== (A) LR-QAOA ===
- MINIMISES: the target is the ground state of H_C ("the ground state encodes the optimal solution", "amplifying solutions with low energy", "our focus is on finding the ground state of the cost Hamiltonian"). Maximisation problems such as (W)MaxCut are first rewritten as an Ising Hamiltonian whose ground state is the optimum.
- Cost unitary: e^{-j gamma H_C} (minus sign). Mixer unitary: e^{+j beta H_B} with H_B = +sum X (plus sign), implemented as R_X(-2 beta) on every qubit. Start state |+>^n. Delta_gamma, Delta_beta positive; gamma increases linearly, beta decreases linearly.
- R_x definition in the paper's Supplementary Note 5, Eq. (20): R_x(theta) = exp(-j theta X/2), the same as Qiskit.
- This is IDENTICAL to our convention (U_C = exp(-i gamma H), U_M = exp(+i beta sum X) = rx(-2 beta), |+>^n start, minimisation). No sign change is needed.

=== (B) SPSA ===
- MINIMISES a loss L(theta) ("The goal is to minimize a loss function L(theta)"); the update subtracts the gradient estimate: theta_{k+1} = theta_k - a_k g_hat_k.
- Iteration counter starts at k = 0 in the formulas (the MATLAB listing loops k = 1..n and therefore writes (k+A) and k instead of (A+k+1) and (k+1)).
- Notation clash: SPSA's alpha and gamma are gain-decay EXPONENTS (0.602, 0.101), unrelated to the QAOA angles gamma, beta. Delta_k in SPSA is the random +-1 vector, unrelated to LR-QAOA's Delta_gamma, Delta_beta.

=== (C) Lucas ===
- MINIMISES the energy H (ground state = solution). With B > 0 the number of cut edges is minimised; B < 0 would maximise it.
- Spins s = +-1; Lucas's bit convention is x = (s + 1)/2 (s = +1 means x = 1), which is the OPPOSITE of ours (z = 1 - 2x, z = +1 means x = 0). For graph partitioning this does not matter because H is invariant under s -> -s and has no linear term; it does matter for other Lucas formulations written in x.
result.parameters:
=== (A) LR-QAOA ===
- Hardware experiments (IonQ, Quantinuum, IBM): Delta_beta = 0.3, Delta_gamma = 0.6. The fixed-parameter simulations of Supplementary Note 3 (4 to 42 qubits, p = 10 to 400) use the same Delta_gamma = 0.6, Delta_beta = 0.3.
- Main simulations: Delta values scanned on ONE instance per problem size and reused for the other 99 instances; "For problems with 20 or fewer qubits, we scan over 6 Delta_beta values and 7 Delta_gamma values, and for more than 20, 4 Delta_beta and 4 Delta_gamma". The grid values themselves are only in Fig. 10 (not read).
- Landscape (Supplementary Note 1, p = 50, Delta from 0 to 3 pi/4): "a Delta_beta <= 0.6 and a Delta_gamma <= 0.6 give favorable results"; the best point is not necessarily Delta_beta = Delta_gamma; excessively large values do not help.
- Trends: Delta for larger p tends to be less than or equal to that for smaller p; with p = N_q on fully connected WMaxCut they used Delta_{gamma,beta} = 0.5 and had to lower it to 0.4 beyond about 25 qubits ("one must reduce Delta_{gamma,beta} as the number of qubits increases").
- All these values assume the NORMALISED Hamiltonian (divide J and h by max|J_ij|; MIS by max|h_i|). The paper says the consistent landscape "is only observed when the Hamiltonian is normalized".

=== (B) SPSA (Spall 1998, Section III.B) ===
- alpha = 0.602, gamma = 0.101 ("effectively the lowest allowable satisfying the theoretical conditions"); asymptotically optimal alternatives 1.0 and 1/6.
- A: "much less than the maximum number of iterations allowed or expected, e.g., we frequently take it to be 10% (or less) of the maximum number of expected/allowed iterations".
- c: "approximately equal to the standard deviation of the measurement noise in y(theta)", estimated from several evaluations at the initial guess; with noise-free measurements, "some small positive number".
- a: chosen so that a/(A+1)^alpha times the magnitude of the elements of g_hat_0(theta_0) is about the smallest desired early change in theta. Worked example in the paper: desired move 0.1, |g_hat_0| about 10, A = 100, alpha = 0.602 gives a = 0.16 (I rechecked: 0.01 * 101^0.602 = 0.161).
- High noise: smaller a and larger c than in a low-noise setting. Footnote 2: averaging two to four independent SP gradient estimates per iteration can help when noise is high.
- Perturbation: symmetric Bernoulli +-1, probability 1/2.

=== (C) Lucas ===
- Penalty weights: A/B >= min(2 Delta, N)/8 with Delta the maximal degree and N the number of vertices (stated for B > 0, as "a rather simple lower bound on A"). Example: B = 1, max degree 4, N = 20 gives A >= 1. For dense graphs (2 Delta >= N) it reduces to A >= B N/8.
- N spins on a complete graph are needed; one spin can be fixed to remove the s -> -s degeneracy.
result.mapping_to_our_convention:
=== (A) LR-QAOA: direct, no sign changes ===
Is "positive Delta_gamma and Delta_beta, gamma ramping UP, beta ramping DOWN" correct for our unitaries and a minimisation problem? YES. The paper uses exactly our unitaries (e^{-j gamma H_C}, e^{+j beta sum X} = R_X(-2 beta), |+>^n) and targets the ground state.
Why (my derivation, not a quote): our mixer is exp(-i beta H_M) with H_M = -sum X, whose ground state is |+>^n. A first-order Trotter step of H(s) = (1-s) H_M + s H gives exp(+i beta sum X) with beta = dt(1-s) >= 0 decreasing, and exp(-i gamma H) with gamma = dt*s >= 0 increasing, so the state follows the ground state from |+>^n to the minimum of H.
Numerical check I ran (not from the paper; script /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-t/7c811c50-f516-4e09-a51a-78bd3f6d1c7e/scratchpad/lit/lr_check.py): 5 random 10-qubit Ising instances (Gaussian J and h, normalised by max|J_ij|), p = 30, Delta_gamma = 0.6, Delta_beta = 0.3, our unitaries and z = 1 - 2x:
  - our direction: mean P(ground state) = 0.435 (uniform = 0.00098), mean <E> = -20.1 against E_min = -21.4;
  - sign of gamma OR beta flipped alone: P(ground) = 0.000, P(highest-energy state) = 0.389 (it maximises instead);
  - both signs flipped: 0.435 again (complex-conjugate circuit);
  - ramps reversed (gamma down, beta up): P(ground) = 0.0009, i.e. no better than uniform.
Schedule for layers k = 1..p (k = i + 1):
  gamma_k = (k/p) * Delta_gamma            -> from Delta_gamma/p up to Delta_gamma
  beta_k  = (1 - (k-1)/p) * Delta_beta     -> from Delta_beta down to Delta_beta/p
Implementation steps:
  1. Build J_ij (i<j) and h_i of E(z); drop the constant.
  2. Normalise: s = max_{i<j} |J_ij|; J' = J/s, h' = h/s. (The paper's alternative when fields dominate: s = max over |h_i| and |J_ij|.)
  3. Circuit: h on every qubit; for k = 1..p: rzz(2*gamma_k*J'_ij) on each coupled pair, rz(2*gamma_k*h'_i) on each qubit, then rx(-2*beta_k) on every qubit. Cost block first, mixer second.
  4. Starting values: Delta_gamma = 0.6, Delta_beta = 0.3; scan both within (0, 0.6] if budget allows, and lower them as n or p grows.
  5. Read out bit x_i and convert with z_i = 1 - 2 x_i (Z|0> = +|0>), consistent with our convention.
The effective angle on the un-normalised H is gamma_k / s.

=== (B) SPSA: direct, it minimises ===
Use it to minimise the measured energy y(theta) = estimated <H> (theta = all 2p angles, or just (Delta_gamma, Delta_beta)). For k = 0..K-1:
  a_k = a/(A + k + 1)^0.602, c_k = c/(k + 1)^0.101
  Delta_k = random vector of +-1 (probability 1/2 each)
  g_k = [y(theta_k + c_k Delta_k) - y(theta_k - c_k Delta_k)]/(2 c_k) * Delta_k   (1/Delta_ki = Delta_ki for +-1 entries)
  theta_{k+1} = theta_k - a_k g_k
Settings: A = 0.1*K (or less); c = standard deviation of the energy estimate at theta_0 at the shot count used (small positive number on a noiseless simulator); a from a/(A+1)^0.602 * |g_0| = desired first-step size. Two circuit evaluations per iteration regardless of the number of parameters. In the notebook rename SPSA's exponents (for example alpha_spsa, gamma_spsa) to avoid confusion with the QAOA angles. If the energy is computed on the normalised H, c and a scale with it.

=== (C) Lucas graph partitioning in our Ising form (expansion is mine, s_i = our z_i) ===
(sum_i s_i)^2 = N + 2 sum_{i<j} s_i s_j, so
  H = sum_{i<j} [ 2A - (B/2) a_ij ] z_i z_j + [ A*N + B*|E|/2 ],  with a_ij = 1 if (i,j) is an edge, else 0.
Therefore J_ij = 2A - B/2 on edges, J_ij = 2A on non-edges, h_i = 0, const = A*N + B*|E|/2. Choose B > 0 and A >= B*min(2*Delta, N)/8.
Check: a balanced partition has H = B * (number of cut edges). All N(N-1)/2 pairs carry a coupling (complete graph). Because h = 0, the bit-convention difference (Lucas x = (s+1)/2 against our z = 1 - 2x) has no effect; the two sides are simply the x = 0 and x = 1 sets. For LR-QAOA the normaliser is max|J_ij| = max(2A, |2A - B/2|).
For weighted edges, replacing a_ij by w_ij and Delta by the maximum weighted degree is my extension, not stated by Lucas.
result.caveats:
(A) LR-QAOA
- Title spelling differs: journal "Toward a linear-ramp QAOA protocol: evidence of ...", arXiv v3 "Towards a Linear-Ramp QAOA protocol: Evidence of ...". Equation numbers differ by one between arXiv v3 and npj (schedule is Eq. (4) in arXiv, Eq. (5) in npj; normalisation is (12) against (13)).
- Internal sign slip in the paper: Eq. (6)-(7) (npj (7)-(8)) write alpha -> e^{j theta} alpha with theta = E_k gamma_t, whereas Eq. (2) e^{-j gamma H_C} implies theta = -E_k gamma_t. The accompanying sentence "Negative energies are rotated counterclockwise" agrees with Eq. (2). Implement Eq. (2); this is my reading, the paper does not comment on it.
- The Delta scan in the paper selects by probability of the optimal bitstring, which requires knowing the optimum. On an unknown instance select by mean or best sampled energy instead (my suggestion).
- The scan-one-instance strategy is described by the authors as "not ideal". The 0.6/0.3 values are not universal: the paper itself lowers Delta for larger N and p.
- Penalty-constrained problems (TSP, BPP) were the weakest cases in the paper; a graph-partitioning Hamiltonian with a large balance penalty A is of that type, and after dividing by max|J| = 2A the objective term is small relative to the penalty.
- My numerical direction check is a 10-qubit, 5-instance sanity test, not a benchmark.
- The first fetch tool summarises pages with a small model; I re-read the raw arXiv HTML and raw Nature HTML locally and the quotes below come from those. One such summary of the Frontiers page returned an inequality "B >= 4A/min(Delta, N/2)" that is NOT in the source and contradicts Eq. (10); disregard it.

(B) SPSA
- Both Spall PDFs are scans without a text layer; the quotes were transcribed by eye from rendered page images, so minor punctuation differences are possible. Bibliographic data was confirmed against Crossref.
- Spall states the guidelines "are just that—guidelines—and may not be the best for every application".
- The 1998 text says the Bernoulli choice is "as suggested in Step 1" although it appears in Step 2; quoted as printed.
- 0.602 and 0.101 follow from the 1992 conditions (alpha - 2 gamma > 0, 3 gamma - alpha/2 >= 0, sum (a_k/c_k)^2 < infinity); that link is my arithmetic (0.602 - 0.101 = 0.501 > 0.5; 3*0.101 = 0.303 >= 0.301), the 1998 paper only cites "Spall [27, prop. 2]".

(C) Lucas
- Eq. (8) is printed with a mismatched index (sum over n of s_i) in both arXiv v3 and the Frontiers PDF; the meaning is sum over i.
- The A/B bound is called "a rather simple lower bound" and is derived for a single constraint violation; at equality the constrained and violating states can tie, so use a margin above the bound (my advice).
- The formulation is for unweighted graphs and an even number of vertices.
- The Frontiers web page lists an internal first-page id (74887); the correct citation is Front. Phys. 2:5 (2014), as printed in the PDF footer ("February 2014 | Volume 2 | Article 5").
